title: Sony Music, Warner sue Anthropic, alleging a “brazen campaign” of intellectual property theft
author: Kirsten Korosec
summary: This latest lawsuit is particularly broad and homes in on accusations of illegal piracy.
full_text:
Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell and numerous other music publishers have sued Anthropic and co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann, alleging the AI lab conducted a “brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works.”

The lawsuit, which was filed late Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, was first reported by Music Business Worldwide . The publishers accuse Anthropic of “blatant theft” by using thousands of copyrighted works to train its AI model Claude.

“We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court,” an Anthropic spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch.

This isn’t the first intellectual property lawsuit Anthropic has faced. Some of the same lawyers behind this lawsuit also represent Concord Music Group and Universal Music Group in a case filed in January and led the Bartz v. Anthropic case, in which a group of authors accused Anthropic of using copyrighted works to train products like Claude. Anthropic was ordered to pay $1.5 billion in the landmark Bartz case after a judge ruled that while it was legal for the AI lab to use copyrighted works, it was not legal to acquire that content through piracy.

While the cases make similar arguments, there are key differences. This latest lawsuit is particularly broad and builds off the other cases, including by accusing Anthropic of “flagrant piracy” through illegal torrenting to obtain millions of copies of books, including those that contain lyrics and sheet music.

title: “We’re not doing 30 bets a year”: Vijay Pande on betting small after running $4 billion at a16z
author: Connie Loizos
summary: Vijay Pande — who left a16z's roughly $4 billion biotech practice last year to start the much smaller, AI-native VZVC — talks about why biology is finally shifting from a "discovery" science to an "engineering" one, why clinical trials are still brutally expensive, and why he thinks open, shared datasets (not walled-off ones) are what will actually let AI transform medicine.
full_text:
It used to be that Vijay Pande was better known in academic circles than investor circles. That changed pretty abruptly a dozen years ago, when Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz — who’d spent their firm’s first five years explicitly avoiding healthcare and life sciences — decided the category was worth betting on after all and handed the keys to Pande. At the time, he was a Stanford chemistry professor who was best known for building Folding@home, the distributed-computing project that turned millions of home PCs into a supercomputer for disease research. Over the next decade-plus, he grew a16z’s bet into a practice managing close to $4 billion.

So it was somewhat unexpected when in June of last year, Pande walked away from it all to start something much smaller. In fact, his new firm, VZVC , co-founded with longtime investor Zach Werner, is built around a handful of concentrated bets a year rather than dozens, it has no associates, and it relies heavily on AI for its day-to-day operations.

To learn more about Pande’s hard pivot, we talked with him this week about why he’s making just a handful of concentrated bets rather than spreading himself thin in the current market — and about one of the more interesting conundrums in AI-driven biotech: unlike text, biological data can’t be scraped off the internet, so nearly every company ends up building its own walled-off dataset. What does that mean for all the advances AI in medicine has promised, and who actually gets access to them?

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. You can also listen to the fuller conversation (below).

You’ve said biology is moving from a “science of discovery” to something you can engineer. What does that mean?

For a lot of the way drugs have been developed, there was very much a fortuitous aspect to it. I think what’s shifted is that AI and machine learning allow computers to wrap their type of understanding around something very, very complicated… to try to figure out what targets you want your drugs to hit, for specific diseases, to be able to make those drugs, and now even to help in the clinical trials — which are the most expensive part of the process.

I thought clinical trials were getting cheaper because drug developers are using more synthetic data, so not as many people are needed for these trials.

That’s, I think, very much an aspiration.

The cost and time to get to clinical trials has been shrinking, especially with AI, but it could still cost hundreds of millions of dollars to run a trial, which is why drugs are very expensive. The probability of a drug going successfully from the first trial to the end of the third trial is just 20%. If 8 out of 10 fail, and these things cost hundreds of millions of dollars, the amortized cost gets really high. The reason they fail typically is not that the biologist did something wrong; it’s that all the experiments these drugs were designed on were on animal models like mice, and in the end, animal models are just not very predictive of humans. The AI model is not going to be perfect, but it’s going to be way better than any animal model would be, and once it crosses that bar, that’s where it gets really exciting.

[The phase after that is]: Is the drug the right drug for me ?

The jargon here is so-called precision medicine. If you go to a doctor with something not trivial, they have to guess what’s going on, because there’s only so much they can tell. Then they give you a drug — and if that doesn’t work, they give you another drug, then another drug. This happens in cancer, it happens in lots of different areas. We would all be much better off if the first drug was the right one. Typically, your blood test values are compared to population averages. But really, they should be compared to: is this [result] weird for you? What we’re starting to do also on the medicine side is [the ability] to just understand what would be right for the individual.

Would you say the path to this moment has been slow and steady, or did it spike more recently?

I think it’s lots of different things [coming together]. So for instance, precision medicine for the longest time was based on genomics. But the reality is your genome is kind of like the blueprint for your house on day one, but your house is fairly different now compared with the moment it was built. So there are many other things that people can now measure in proteomics and so on that are much more relevant for understanding disease and where your body is now. There has also been [a lot of] automation in robotic measurements that is naturally tied into AI, and those two go hand in hand really well.

Over the last decade, there’s been this steady clip fforin both AI for biology and AI for chemistry. The biology part is like, how can we treat this disease? And then the chemistry part is, how can we come up with a drug to go after that specific protein? There have actually been very significant advances over those 10 years.

You mentioned that biology is one of the few places AI can’t just scrape data off the internet. What does that mean for how the field develops?

It’s a place where you don’t have any of this data that people can just all train the same thing, and your data can’t be distilled from one model to another. It’s a really interesting play from just the pure AI sense.

Doesn’t that echo a familiar problem in medicine, though — doctors operating in [territorial, often competitive] silos?

You’re onto something really big here. Let’s say [someone] has some type of cancer, and it’s both an issue in oncology and endocrinology — those two doctors really don’t sync together very well. What is really intriguing about AI is that it can, in principle, be a specialist in everything, and it can start to see things that really any single human being couldn’t. It would be equivalent to having a team of the very best doctors all clamoring together in that moment.

But is there enough data sharing for that vision to actually be realized? I understand why founders and investors want to protect their [respective findings], but . . .

I think one of the bigger trends is that we’re starting to see a shift toward building these atlases of biological information — which, from a technology standpoint, are typically foundation models. And as they become more common, I think we’ll see the same thing that’s happened with open-source LLMs, which do very well against the corporate ones: open-source foundation models in biology having a very broad impact.

You’re involved with Genesis Therapeutics, which came out of your lab at Stanford, and Insitro, the drug-discovery company launched by Daphne Koller, a former colleague at Stanford. You say you’re also incubating a company with a founder you’ve known for 20 years. What are you looking for in founders, and in what areas?

There are two areas that I’ve been spending most of my time on. One is AI for healthcare delivery, which I did a ton at a16z as well, and then AI for clinical trials.

One of the things that’s most important to me [about founders] is that we can really trust each other — founders that have high integrity, that do what they say they’re gonna do… I’m expecting this relationship to be 5, 10 years plus into, ideally, their next company. I want to work with people who are thinking long term like that. Ideally, these are people who are not just trying to win and beat other people, but really thinking about the question: how do we win together?

What have you gotten right and wrong in your investing career so far?

When I started talking about AI and machine learning and technology and medicine and bio 10 plus years ago, there was a lot of resistance and a lot of people saying, ‘Oh, that’s never going to happen. That’s never going to be useful,’ and so on. That resistance is largely gone and seeing this arc is very fulfilling.

I think it took me some time to really appreciate that as seductive as the coolest technologies are, it really always comes back to go-to-market. I tell my founders, especially the ones who are coming from the science or the product side, for them to take all their brilliance and creativity and really apply it to the go-to-market side, that the go-to-market part is at least as hard or harder than the technology side.

Help us understand how you’re designing this new firm differently, compared with what you were running at a16z.

Right now, we’re doing something really quite different… VZ is named after me, Vijay, and my co-founder, Zach Werner — he’s the Z. We’re intentionally really quite small… on the investment side, it’s really just the two of us. We were actually intending on hiring associates, but it turned out, with the agents that we’ve built up, not to be something that we need to do.

We’re [not] driving 30 bets per year… we’re talking about probably five, not a lot of investments — very concentrated. Adding a company at a typical fund is like adding a Facebook friend — that’s something you do pretty quickly. For Zach and I, it’s more like  . . . wanting to have another child. This is a big deal for us.

With that structure, who are you competing against for deals?

The funny thing about this model is that typically we’re not trying to compete for a hot round — people make room for us. It’s a very different thing than trying to get the hot Series A or Series B. Largely, people want us as investors because of what Zach and I can do, and how hands-on we can be. When I look at people who are inspirations, I look at someone like Antonio Gracias at Valor — he’s well-known now because of the SpaceX deal, but he’s been doing what he’s been doing for 20 years. What Thrive has done, with a more concentrated portfolio, is also a real inspiration. Obviously, a16z is sort of in my DNA as well, but I think those other ones are new additions to how we think about things.

What’s overhyped right now in AI and biotech?

The reality is that AI can find insights that we can’t get from just humans alone. The thing that always gets tricky is when there’s this call that AI is going to cure all everything. The reason for hesitance there is not because of any doubt about AI — it’s about doubt of the data. LLMs work because there’s so much data to learn from. When the data is just simply not there, then AI can’t magically solve that problem.

title: Nvidia’s AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
author: Russell Brandom
summary: The new generation of data center systems is increasing efficiency with smarter traffic control instead of just more processor cycles.
full_text:
Before this week, the dominant story about Nvidia went something like this: For the first few years of the AI boom, Nvidia was the only source for state-of-the-art GPUs, which became immensely profitable as the industry scaled out. In the last few years, hyperscalers like Amazon and Google have started building their own chips, and Nvidia is no longer the only game in town, leading many investors to wonder how durable its advantage really is.

It’s a compelling story, and mostly true. After growing its market cap 10x between the start of 2023 and mid-2025, Nvidia shares have been on a more modest trajectory for the past year, driven by concerns about GPU competition.

A new narrative has taken shape since the company’s earnings on Wednesday and investors are starting to realize that Nvidia’s advantage goes far beyond GPUs. As AI’s compute grows into the gigawatt scale, orchestration has become an increasingly complex task. Not surprisingly, Nvidia has built much of the state-of-the-art hardware needed to handle it, giving the company a huge advantage in the systems that surround the GPU even as it sees increased competition on the GPUs themselves.

For all the talk of compute as a commodity , it’s still incredibly difficult to operate a megascale data center at peak efficiency — and as deployments get bigger and faster, that challenge is only growing.

You can see some of this just by looking at the details of what Nvidia is actually selling. The company is currently rolling out its Vera Rubin architecture, which pairs the Rubin GPU with a collection of other units, including the Vera CPU, the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator and similar racks for storage and networking.

Over the past week, I’ve been talking to folks at Nvidia about what those systems actually do, and the results have been surprising. Like the Rubin GPU itself, they’re extremely specialized systems, but instead of churning through tokens, they’re making sure everything outside the GPU works as efficiently as possible. If the GPU is the engine, these are the rest of the car.

The Vera CPU in particular is focused on the problem of orchestrating data. “Vera is important because there’s only so much memory that you can put in a single server or any sort of compute platform,” Jason Hardy, Nvidia’s VP of storage technology, told me.

As data centers have scaled up computing power, memory capacity has scaled up too, which is why companies like Micron have gotten rich in the second wave of the infrastructure boom. But getting that data to the GPU at the right time isn’t straightforward — and as companies look to drive tokens-per-watt lower and lower, they’re realizing how important that kind of traffic direction is.

“We saw upwards of 3x improvement in these operations, where the Vera CPU is allowing for acceleration,” Hardy said. “So now we can use our flash to its fullest potential, because we can get all that performance out of it without bottlenecking.”

You can see versions of the same problem outside of Nvidia. When OpenAI developed its Jalapeño chip, a major focus was avoiding these challenges entirely by minimizing the amount of data that needs to be moved around.

“We designed Jalapeño to minimize data movement and communication delays,” the company said in a blog post earlier this month . “Its large domain allows the entire workload to remain within one connected system, minimizing data movement and helping the complete request stay fast and efficient from beginning to end.”

It’s a different approach, avoiding data movement entirely by conducting a workload within one integrated chip. But the overall logic is the same, increasing efficiency with smarter traffic control instead of just more processor cycles. That in turn opens up a whole new layer of infrastructure for companies to compete over.

This new focus on data orchestration isn’t automatically a win for Nvidia. The company will have to compete with rival chipmakers and hyperscalers just as it has with GPUs. But the competition has moved to a new layer, where building a rival GPU matters less than being able to make the entire system work efficiently.

And at least in the early stages, Nvidia looks to have a commanding lead.

I used to be an avid hiker and would try to go backpacking a few times a year. I always dreamed of thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail, but life kind of got in the way. (Turns out jobs, wives, and children aren’t thrilled with the idea of you disappearing for three months.) But I’ve been longing to reconnect with my love of the outdoors and just recently took my kids on their first camping trip. So I discovered A Trail Tale at a really opportune time. It’s an interactive trail journal created by Andy Moliski with help from his brothers Adam and Alex.

The various segments of the trail are rendered in beautiful pixel art reminiscent of a ‘90s Sierra point-and-click adventure. Alex recorded an equally gorgeous original score that combines nature sounds, acoustic guitar, strings, and even what sounds like clarinet.

As you click through each day, you’re greeted with information about landmarks and a game-like UI that is partially inspired by titles like Oregon Trail. (Spoiler: nobody dies of dysentery in this one.) Clicking on Andy unfurls a menu of icons that offer details about the journey, his mental state, and even bits of poetry. There are even little icons for things that impact his fortitude and morale meters, like inclement weather or picturesque scenery.

It’s insanely easy to just get lost in Andy’s journey for hours. And it’s making me wonder if I should get back out there and start tackling some more of the AT myself.

Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday, and today the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Reuters and the Washington Post that he had been deported to the UK. Yiannopoulos came to the US legally in 2019, but overstayed his visa. After he failed to appear in court for an immigration hearing, a final order of removal was issued ​on July 22.

The British national made a name for himself as an editor at Steve Bannon’s Breitbart and an early supporter of Donald Trump’s. He has had a long history of controversial statements and associations, including reportedly helping arrange Trump’s dinner with Kanye West and white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and he was a key figure in the online harassment campaign Gamergate .

In recent years, however, his antics have led to a falling out with most significant figures on the right, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer. He has denied condoning statutory rape or pedophilia , but he has suggested it’s acceptable for an adult to have a sexual relationship with a 13-year-old .

There’s no word if the 44 interns in a trenchcoat who also constitute the entity known as Milo Yiannopoulos have also been deported.

Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for “tens of thousands” copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance when identifiable copyright data was stripped. In total, the damages could amount to several billion dollars if a court finds in Sony and Warner’s favor and awards the maximum amount.

This is just the latest high-profile suit against Anthropic, which recently settled a suit brought by the publishing industry for $1.5 billion . It’s also faced multiple lawsuits from Universal Music Group, Concord, and ABKCO, plus separate suits from BMG and Round Hill Music .

In addition to suing Anthropic as an entity, the complaint names Co-Founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The suit alleges that Mann used BitTorrent to download over five million pirated books , and that employees downloaded at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror . It also claims that Anthropic scraped lyrics from sites like MusixMatch and LyricFind, which paid to license content from the labels.

Plaintiff Music Publishers, a group of the world’s leading music publishers, bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history. Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s “Claude” series of artificial intelligence (“AI”) models.

Specific songs named as being found in Anthropic’s training data include Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ On a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” and TaylorSwift’s “Paper Rings.” Antrhopic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel.

Balancing the wants and needs of these more demanding users has been a challenge that BYOK founder Nick Sjolinder has been trying to figure out how to tackle. The answer he seems to have landed on, is scripts. Rather than clutter BYOK with a ton of features that 80 percent of its users wont touch, or crowd the Studio app with even more formats, the company is planning to implement optional scripts that expand the capabilities of BYOK.

A few examples of the kinds of thing people will be able to create are a screenplay assistant, a character note tool, and a writing analyzer. This could let users highlight text in a document and pull it out as a note or tell them when they’re using the passive voice. It’s still early in development and the scripting features haven’t rolled out publicly, but BYOK is asking for feedback from its users.

Joseph Fink is the cocreator and cowriter of Welcome to Night Vale , arguably the most important fiction podcast ever. He’s also the creator of the noir podcast Unlicensed and Alice Isn’t Dead , which takes some of the conspiratorial cosmic horror of Night Vale and turns it into fodder for a more serious series about relationships, trauma, and the open road. There’s also a sequel series out now called Don’t Tell Alice that takes the story down an even darker path in which protagonist Keisha is the one with a secret.

Joseph is also an accomplished author. In addition to co-writing the three Welcome to Night Vale novels, he’s also penned the Alice Isn’t Dead novel and The Halloween Moon . His latest work is The Nudge , which features some gorgeous illustrations from Jessica Hayworth, who also provides the art for Night Vale , hits shelves on September 1st. It’s a brief and unsettling novella about a man trying to outrun some mysterious evil.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

Podcast Addict. It’s an Android-only podcast app made by one guy named Xavier, and it is so much better than any other podcast app that it’s the main reason I can never switch to an iPhone. I’m maybe the one guy in the entire country who chooses phones based on how they play podcasts.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I use Bluesky, which I used to like because no one was there and so no one read my posts, which is really the ideal social media for me. Now there are more people there, and sometimes people read and respond to my posts, which is a drag.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

My entire understanding of storytelling is probably shaped by Grim Fandango , a 1999 adventure game about a sad sack grim reaper navigating a film noir afterlife. There are lines and images from that game that will live in my head forever, even if a lot of them were parodies or references to classic films I wasn’t even aware existed when I first played that game.

Our Audible show Unlicensed was one of those few projects that turned out exactly how I wanted it to in my head. A mystery series set in the least cool parts of Los Angeles, the parts where the actual people live. I didn’t want it to be “good for two writers who usually don’t write mysteries.” I just wanted us to write a damn good mystery, and I think we did. We got three seasons out of Audible, but then they mostly shut down their original shows department, and that was it. If I had my choice though, I’d happily spend the rest of my life writing Unlicensed .

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

I recently watched a talk with Meshell Ndegeocello, and she described having to shush a fellow student in a guitar workshop who was noodling on his guitar while the teacher was trying to demonstrate something. Meshell said: “As a musician, it doesn’t matter how well you play if you can’t listen.” I don’t know if it’s the best advice I’ve ever received, but I think it’s damn good advice and applies to a lot of things outside of music.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I buy too many books, constantly. I like to hang out in bookstores, and I’ve never left one without buying at least a couple of books. I’m mostly not a physical media guy, I have no interest in owning records or DVDs, but I’ll build an addition to my house before I get rid of any books.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“It turns out watching a guy write audio fiction on his computer is boring, this movie was a mistake sorry, we’re sorry.”

I don’t really use GIFs or memes. I’m very much a text guy, which is why I stick to text social media mostly, even though that doesn’t really help you sell books or stuff like that.

What do you want from a flip phone when it’s closed? A simple interface, perhaps notifications and a widget or two, for handling the basics? Or a fully fledged Android experience shrunk down for the Flip form factor? For years, Samsung has insisted on the former, even as some fans — and Razr rival Motorola — have pushed for the latter. With the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Samsung has given in.

Although the Z Flip 8’s hardware is almost unchanged year-on-year, Samsung has fundamentally rethought how this phone is meant to be used when shut. The cover screen feels more like a regular Android phone, with easier access to the full versions of every single app, letting you browse social media, watch movies, and play games without ever opening the phone. Not every app works well on a tiny square screen with two cameras in the middle of it, but even when they don’t, that friction between me and the distractions of my phone still feels as much a feature as a bug.

Everything exciting about the Z Flip 8 lies in its 4-inch cover screen, which is now more versatile than ever thanks to a homescreen redesign. Swiping down from the top left now brings up your notifications, while swiping from the top right instead shows a cover-screen-optimized version of the Quick Settings panel. Immediately, this feels more like a phone.

More exciting is what happens when you swipe up from the bottom: you get an app drawer. By default, this is populated with a selection of Samsung’s own apps that are optimized for the square screen, plus a “Labs” section with third-party options including Netflix and WhatsApp. But right below that , Samsung has included an easy prompt to install MultiStar, the Good Lock module that lets you run any app you’d like on the outer screen.

Samsung used to bury the option deep in the phone’s settings, only to be found by those who knew to look for it. The bottom of the app drawer isn’t quite front and center, but it’s much more prominent than it used to be.

You can still run apps in three forms: full-screen, with the cameras blocking part of the software; a square display that stops just above the level of the cameras; or a thin portrait-aspect ratio that letterboxes the sides. A small virtual button at the bottom of the screen lets you cycle through them.

Good performance isn’t guaranteed. Some apps, like Withings’ health tracker companion app, are almost impossible to use on the cover screen, with no configuration that leaves enough space for its graphs to fit. Google Maps is only a bit better — I love the idea of quickly checking my walking route without opening the phone, but there are so many floating interface elements that it’s unwieldy at best. Others work smoothly, but feel pointless: I can stream HBO Max on the tiny outer display, but I’d never want to.

But for other apps, the new cover screen options feel genuinely freeing. I can open Todoist and tick off a task, dip into WhatsApp to send a message, or open MyFitnessPal to log the snack I just ate. They’re quick actions that work well enough on the small screen, and because other apps — *cough* Instagram *cough* — don’t, I can dive into them without the risk of getting dragged into doomscrolling. That little bit of friction is just enough to save me from wasting 20 minutes I’ll never get back.

As for the hardware, little has changed. The Z Flip 8 is 0.6mm thinner and 8g lighter than its predecessor. This is the thickest of Samsung’s three current foldables, but it’s more compact than Motorola’s Razrs , its only real rivals.

Samsung didn’t upgrade the Z Flip 8 with the thinner, tougher titanium display stack found in the two new Z Fold 8 phones, which also means this has just as visible a crease as ever. It rarely bothers me, and is hard to see head-on, but you may feel differently. The IP48 rating is a more objective issue, and means that while this phone is mostly safe from water, it’s still vulnerable to dust.

On the inside, you’ll find the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 if you’re in the US, though my UK model runs Samsung’s Exynos 2600. Exynos chips get a bad rep, but performance has been smooth so far, and I have no real complaints.

As with the Z Fold 8 phones, Samsung switched to more energy-dense silicon-carbon batteries for the Z Flip 8. Unlike those phones, it didn’t actually increase the battery capacity, but instead used smaller cells with the same 4,300mAh capacity — the key to shrinking the phone itself. Still, battery life is solid, reliably lasting the full day with battery to spare. The charging — 25W wired, 15W wireless — is relatively unimpressive, and the only way to get Qi2 charging is still by using a compatible magnetic case.

Storage and RAM remain the same as on the Z Flip 7; the screens do too apart from small bumps to peak brightness, and the cameras are also identical to last year’s. The 50-megapixel main camera is impressive, and especially helpful since the form factor means you can use it for selfies too. The 12-megapixel ultrawide and 10-megapixel inner camera aren’t remarkable, but they get the job done. A slab phone at this price would have better cameras, and most likely a telephoto lens, but the lenses here are good enough.

The question is whether it’s all good enough for the price, given Samsung has bumped the Z Flip 8 up to $1,199.99, a $100 increase. Z Flip 7 owners certainly shouldn’t upgrade, and anyone else should consider buying that phone instead, since the difference between the two is slight.

After all, the big upgrades are software, and unlikely to remain exclusive. Last year’s Z Flip 7 hasn’t yet been updated to One UI 9, but since its outer screen is almost identical, it seems likely to get the upgraded software, giving one less reason to opt for the new model. The Z Flip 6 and earlier, with their smaller cover screens, seem more likely to miss out. I’ve asked Samsung about its upgrade plans, but haven’t yet heard back.

Most of the other software upgrades aren’t even Flip-specific. Customizable, AI-powered cards have been added to the daily Now Brief; My FanCam lets you crop video to focus on a specific subject; and Audio Eraser can now dim background noise and highlight dialogue in apps like YouTube and Netflix. You’ll find those features across all of Samsung’s new foldables, plus the new Galaxy S26 FE .

Modest as the Z Flip 8’s hardware upgrades are, it feels like a turning point for Samsung, which is mostly done trying to limit the ways people use the cover screen. Given the speculation that the short, wide Z Fold 8 could replace the Flip form factor as Samsung’s “small phone that unfolds to a big phone,” it makes sense to close the gap between them.

The Z Fold 8 is a more capable phone than the Z Flip 8 when closed, its squat screen more usable than the Flip’s tiny one, despite Samsung’s software upgrades. But I have a real soft spot for the Flip form factor, which is tiny and pocketable when closed and a normal, almost compromise-free flagship phone when open — and endlessly satisfying to flip shut.

More than that, I enjoy its frictions. I welcome Samsung’s move to make it easier to use full apps on the cover screen, but I also welcome that it will never be entirely successful. Some apps simply don’t work on a screen this size, and the Z Flip 8 is all the better for it.

summary: As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated, the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI, others have denied using the technology […]

As AI infiltrates the electronic dance music scene, a callout culture is brewing.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated , the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI , others have denied using the technology until increasing public scrutiny forced them to tell the truth .

For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art.

When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit.

“I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.”

Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right.

“Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.”

In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like.

“Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.”

Harris pointed to MANSA’s “ Midnight on My Mind ” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “ Take Me (To The Moon) ” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online.

“People are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking [AI] to remix them.”

Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out.

“Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.”

In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music , but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos . There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop.

Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks.

“These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash . “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.”

Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists.

“Music production is where most of my income comes from, and almost as soon as AI began rolling out, I started losing many of my clients,” said Young, who has previously done audio mixing and mastering work for Sony Music, Warner, and Universal. “I can only imagine what it’s been like for singers, graphics artists, and people working in other creative fields. Whether you realize it or not, this stuff is impacting everyone.”

What Young wishes more listeners could appreciate is how easy it has become to generate entire songs with platforms like Suno. In his opinion, most people using AI to make music “aren’t actually doing anything creative and they don’t have a true artistic process” because many generative tools on the market involve some degree of autogeneration. When I brought up how detailed AI prompts can be, he insisted that many of the people posting AI music likely aren’t even writing their own inputs. Young noted that Suno’s Simple Mode allows users to whip up songs by simply selecting a musical genre and clicking a button — a process that requires basically zero thinking. (Suno has not responded to a request for comment in time for publication.)

As much as traditional artists might loathe generative production, there is no denying that AI songs are making their way into the mainstream. In 2024, Metro Boomin took shots at Drake with a beat sampling comedian King Willonius’ “ BBL Drizzy ” — an AI track whose vocals, melodies, and instrumental elements were generated by AI music startup Udio . Metro Boomin’s “BBL Drizzy” went viral after the producer posted the beat to SoundCloud and invited other performers to rap over it . Drake subsequently rapped over the beat himself on Sexyy Red’s “U My Everything,” and that song managed to peak at 44 on the Billboard Hot 100 .

“I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food.”

Wholly AI-generated songs (and people) are finding success, as well. Last summer, Vinih Pray’s Suno-created song “A Million Colors” also peaked at 44 on TikTok’s Viral 50 chart , and AI artists Breaking Rust and Cain Walker made it onto Billboard’s Country Digital Song sales chart — a lesser-known chart focusing on individual song downloads. Meanwhile, Hallwood Media — a label founded by former Geffen Records president Neil Jacobson — signed AI avatar Xania Monet to a $3 million recording deal . Certain segments of the industry are clearly trying to normalize AI-generated music, and people are definitely making money with their machine-generated tracks. Kapwing estimates that the top 10 most followed / streamed AI music creators on Spotify and YouTube collectively raked in over $6 million in 2025 . And with platforms like Deezer reporting that AI songs now account for over 50 percent of new uploads , that kind of music is getting harder for listeners to avoid — if they can even recognize it. While streaming platforms are beginning to more clearly label AI songs, many listeners have reported that they can’t really hear the difference between generative and human-made music.

Aside from the people uploading all of these songs, no one has a way of being absolutely certain whether the tracks were generated with AI or made by an actual artist. AI music detection tools are one potential solution , but it’s not entirely clear how and, perhaps more importantly, if listeners might incorporate them into their lives. Judging by the numbers (which, of course, can be manipulated with paid streams), there do seem to be people who don’t mind the sounds of Suno and other AI tools. Young knows that most people’s ears probably aren’t well-attuned to identifying audio slop, but he still thinks that music lovers owe it to themselves to make the effort to find real, human artists.

“In my opinion, it becomes obvious that you’re listening to AI-generated music when you put on a good pair of headphones,” Young told me. “But I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food and listening to it through the speakers on their phone. Or they just have it on a background noise, and they don’t necessarily care what it sounds like.”

title: Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
author: Andrew Williams
summary: Burnt out on wrist buzzes and notification overload? A new crop of minimalist wearables promises to collect your health data without demanding your attention.
full_text:
There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable . You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.

They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air , Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series , the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg . One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good .

I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra , a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen , it—like a Fitbit Air —wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.

Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up . When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.

Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.

Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two , but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.

The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.

Whoop has made screen-free wearables since its first proper release in 2015 , but the shift in what Whoop considers itself to be about mirrors the change we see in the wider market. Today a Whoop band is made for just about anyone with the spare cash to pay for its $199 annual subscription. It’s a system to “help you improve how you sleep, train, and feel—starting day one,” to use Whoop’s own words. This couldn’t be further removed from the self-serious way Whoop described itself in 2015, as a “performance optimization system exclusively designed for elite athletes and teams.” What a change a decade makes.

Even if Whoop has always been grounded in the now-common concept of “ training readiness ,” things have altered drastically. So while it’s tempting to say Google's Fitbit and company are playing catch-up with Whoop, that’s not quite it. It has homed in on the “low-distraction” lifestyle selling point just as the other bigger tech companies have.

On at least three fronts this can be attributed—or blamed—on AI, to some extent.

AI is a way for these wearable companies to upsell and make money, and on the other side, a major contributor to why a lot of us feel like we need low-distraction tech these days in the first place. While virtually every Whoop rival says it can be used without a subscription, some of these companies lean heavily on AI as an upsell.

Take Google and the Fitbit Air. Without a subscription, the app looks cute enough but is fairly spare. You get stats and charts, but if you want chatty explainers of what any of it means , you need Google Health Premium at $10 a month. Numbers and graph lines become paragraphs that reference specific quirks or events of the day because, to steal a line from humorist and podcaster John Hodgman, specificity is the soul of narrative.

And this is just the beginning. “The use of AI in monitoring and guiding health and wellness is still at the early stage of development but will likely become significantly more advanced as AI matures,” says Peter Richardson, vice president and cofounder of Counterpoint Research .

I find Google Fitbit’s chatbot ramblings quite annoying, with not-that-rare dips into the condescending, and I may even prefer the subscription-free experience. But my job has pushed me through the unenviable task of learning what VO2 Max actually means, what heart-rate variability trends indicate, and so on: not the norm.

AI could solve that long-standing issue with wearables—people glazing over data as soon as they see anything more than their daily step count. This AI use will be better represented on the phone than the watch screen, too, making the lack of screen a strength. It lets the AI shine.

The most important influence of AI here is on the other side of the equation, though, as just the latest stage in the tech-ification of our daily lives. I’ve heard from multiple friends about how their recent work appraisals focused on higher-ups demanding greater AI use within their “personal workflow.” Perhaps you’ve had a similar experience .

Elizabeth Marsh, a doctoral researcher at the University of Nottingham who studies the dark side of the digital workplace , finds that digital tools consistently trigger a familiar cluster of harms: technostress, information overload, constant interruption, and blurred work–home boundaries.

“These appear to have become the predictable by-product of environments where the volume and pace of digital demand has risen faster than people's capacity to absorb it,” Marsh tells WIRED, noting that information overload and FOMO correlate strongly with lower well-being and higher strain.

It’s a good argument for not having notifications and alerts pop up on your wrist, phone, and work PC—and wherever else your to-do list of responsibilities takes on a digital form.

“Participants described them in visceral terms—one said the notifications “make me feel sometimes on edge and it does make me feel anxious and it affects my mental health;” another described feeling angry at the sender for taking their time, while simultaneously feeling bad for not replying immediately,” Marsh says about her study on “digital workplace technology intensity.”

But she found simply cutting off notifications wasn’t necessarily a solution either, as people worried they would miss something. Screen-free wearables are a parallel development to this kind of tech cold turkey of banishing wearables from your wrist entirely. You can still get your sleep scores and step count, but without it being advertised consciously through the day. With a Garmin Cirqa, you can even see maps of runs and walks without ever having tapped a “start workout” button. Nothing needs to buzz away or, at a simpler level, require the daily charge coddling of an Apple Watch .

This is perhaps the key. So many tech companies are making these low-distraction wearables because so many of us are close to wanting to opt out altogether, at least in the areas of tech in which we can.

Marsh’s suggested strategy for dealing with tech strain is what she calls “ digital mindfulness ,” which is all about having an “awareness of how you engage with technology, rather than operating on autopilot.” That mindless social media feed scrolling? In most cases, you won't convince anyone that’s a digitally mindful practice. Marsh says it involves three things.

“Intention—having a clear purpose for picking up the device in the first place, rather than reaching for it reflexively and then wondering where twenty minutes went,” she says. “Attention—staying with what you've chosen to do and resisting the pull of whatever else is competing for your attention. And attitude—responding to yourself with a bit of kindness and patience when it goes wrong, as self-criticism about our own tech habits tends to make the relationship worse rather than better.”

Buying a screen-free tracker like a Fitbit Air isn’t digital mindfulness in itself. But it’s more intuitively compatible with adopting that mindset than a notification-spewing, buzzing smartwatch.

title: Compliance Is a Data Model: Designing Nigerian Data Systems for the NDPA 2023, GAID 2025 and the…
author: Zigo Business Solutions Ltd
summary: The NDPA is not only a problem for lawyers. Data minimisation, retention, residency, consent, AI governance and data-subject rights should influence the way Nigerian engineers design databases from day one. Compliance Is a Data Model: Designing Nigerian Data Systems for the NDPA 2023, GAID 2025 and the Cloud Era Why Nigerian organisations should stop treating data protection as a legal document and start implementing it in their schemas, pipelines and platforms Most conversations about data protection begin with privacy policies, consent forms and legal teams. For data engineers, architects and developers, that is already too late. By the time an organisation discovers that it cannot easily identify why a customer’s data was collected, where copies of it are stored, which application has access to it, when it should be deleted, or whether it has been transferred outside Nigeria, the real problem is rarely the privacy policy. The problem is often the data model . Nigeria’s data-protection environment has evolved significantly. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, or NDP Act, is now the country’s central statutory framework for personal-data protection. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission, or NDPC, subsequently issued the General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 — GAID 2025 — to translate many of the Act’s principles into more operational requirements. GAID was issued on 20 March 2025 and came fully into force on 19 September 2025. ( National Drug Policy Committee ) At the same time, Nigeria is expanding its cloud, digital sovereignty and data-governance framework through NITDA. Its current regulatory catalogue includes the National Cloud Policy, cloud technical guidelines, interoperability standards and newer cloud-computing guidance. ( NITDA ) For technology teams, this creates an important question: What should a Nigerian data model actually look like if privacy, AI, analytics and regulatory compliance are requirements rather than afterthoughts? The answer requires us to rethink what we mean by data modelling. Data protection should begin before CREATE TABLE A traditional application data model might begin with something like: Customer -------- CustomerId FirstName LastName Email Phone DateOfBirth Address NIN CreatedDate Technically, there is nothing unusual about this model. From a privacy-engineering perspective, however, several questions are unanswered. Why are we collecting DateOfBirth? Does this application really need NIN? Which business process requires Address? Which fields are necessary to execute the contract with the customer, and which were collected merely because “we might need them later”? Can marketing use the same email address? When should each field be deleted? Is the information replicated into a data lake? Has it entered an AI vector database? Does a support vendor outside Nigeria have access to it? Which lawful basis supports each processing activity? That is where the Nigerian regulatory framework becomes directly relevant to data architecture. Section 24 of the NDP Act establishes principles including fairness, lawfulness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; storage limitation; accuracy; security; and accountability. The NDPC summarises these principles as requiring data to be collected for specified and legitimate purposes, limited to what is necessary, kept no longer than required, and appropriately secured. ( erp.ndpc.gov.ng ) GAID makes the engineering implication even clearer. Its guidance states that “minimum necessary” means the least possible data essential to fulfilling the specified purpose and requires controllers and processors to maintain clear retention policies. That means a good Nigerian data model should answer not only: What does this column contain? It should also answer: Why are we allowed to have this column at all? Model the purpose, not just the person A common modelling mistake is attaching every available piece of information to a giant Customer table. A stronger design separates the identity of the individual from the purposes for which different pieces of information are being processed. For example: DataSubject ----------- SubjectId PrimaryIdentifier CreatedAt ProcessingPurpose ----------------- PurposeId PurposeName Description LawfulBasis Owner ActiveFrom ActiveTo DataAttribute ------------- AttributeId AttributeName Classification IsPersonalData IsSensitive EncryptionRequired ProcessingActivity ------------------ ActivityId SubjectId AttributeId PurposeId SourceSystem DestinationSystem CollectedAt RetentionPolicyId This looks more complicated than simply adding fields to Customer. That complexity is intentional. It allows an organisation to answer: “Why do we hold this information?” without searching through Confluence pages, contracts, emails and privacy policies. GAID explicitly expects organisations to understand and document their processing activities and makes reference to Records of Processing Activities, or ROPA, as an important accountability mechanism. ( National Drug Policy Committee ) A mature data architecture can make ROPA partially machine-generated instead of manually reconstructed once a year for compliance. That is an enormous architectural advantage. Lawful basis belongs closer to the data One of the most useful changes Nigerian organisations can make is to stop treating consent as the universal answer to privacy. Consent is one lawful basis, but it is not the only one. Depending on the processing activity, organisations may rely on grounds such as contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest, vital interest, public interest or consent. The NDPC itself demonstrates this approach in its privacy policy by mapping categories of processing to the applicable legal basis. ( erp.ndpc.gov.ng ) This suggests a simple architectural pattern: ProcessingPurpose ----------------- PurposeId Name LawfulBasisType LegalReference RequiresConsent RequiresDPIA AllowsSecondaryUse Owner ReviewDate Now consider what happens when a developer writes: SELECT Email FROM Customer WHERE ... In a conventional system, the database knows who the customer is but knows nothing about why the email is being used. In a more mature architecture, applications should request data within a defined processing context. Conceptually: Application ↓ Processing Purpose ↓ Authorised Data Attributes ↓ Customer Data Marketing, fulfilment, fraud detection and customer support may all use the same customer record, but they should not automatically inherit identical rights to every attribute. That is purpose-based access control , and it may become increasingly important as organisations deploy AI agents capable of traversing multiple enterprise systems. Build retention into the model One of the most expensive phrases in enterprise data management is: “We keep everything.” It sounds safe. From a data-protection perspective, it may be exactly the opposite. GAID states that once the specified and legitimate purpose for retaining personal data has been fulfilled, the legitimate ground for retaining it may cease to exist. It also expects clear data-retention or storage policies. The engineering response should therefore be something more useful than a PDF titled Data_Retention_Policy_Final_v6.pdf. Retention should become data. For example: RetentionPolicy --------------- RetentionPolicyId DataCategory RetentionTrigger RetentionDuration LegalBasis ActionOnExpiry ArchiveAllowed AnonymisationAllowed PolicyOwner LastReviewed A record could then carry: CollectedAt PurposeCompletedAt RetentionPolicyId ScheduledDeletionAt DeletedAt DeletionMethod Now an Azure Data Factory pipeline, Databricks job, Fabric notebook or database procedure can automatically identify records that have passed their approved retention period. Compliance becomes executable. Erasure changes how you design relationships Nigeria’s framework gives data subjects rights including access, rectification, objection, portability, restriction, erasure and protections relating to automated decision-making. ( National Drug Policy Committee ) These rights introduce an architectural question: Can you actually locate one person’s data? Imagine a customer exists in: CRM Payment platform SQL database Data warehouse Blob storage Application logs Support system Marketing platform Vector database Analytics lakehouse AI conversation history Backups Deleting the Customer row solves very little. This is why organisations need a durable internal identifier that can establish lineage across systems. Something like: SubjectIdentityMap ------------------ SubjectId System ExternalIdentifier RecordLocation DataClassification LastSynchronized From there, a Data Subject Request can become a controlled workflow rather than a manual investigation. DataSubjectRequest ------------------ RequestId SubjectId RequestType ReceivedAt VerifiedAt DueAt Status SystemsAffected CompletedAt EvidenceLocation The regulatory requirement therefore creates a very practical data-engineering requirement: personal-data lineage. Your data catalogue should know where the data physically lives Nigeria’s cross-border rules make data location an architectural attribute, not merely an infrastructure decision. GAID states that cross-border transfer may rely on mechanisms including an adequacy decision by the Commission, an approved Cross-Border Data Transfer Instrument, or other lawful bases recognised by the framework. Consequently, an enterprise catalogue should contain more than: Server = prod-sql-01 A more useful model would include: DataLocation ------------ LocationId Provider Service Country Region DataClassification ContainsPersonalData ContainsSensitiveData TransferMechanismId EncryptionAtRest EncryptionInTransit KeyLocation Then: CrossBorderTransfer ------------------- TransferId SourceCountry DestinationCountry PurposeId DataCategories TransferMechanism ApprovalReference StartDate ReviewDate Processor This becomes particularly important in architectures involving Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, SaaS platforms and global AI APIs. Sending information to an API endpoint can itself form part of a data flow. Cloud architecture diagrams therefore need a new question beside every arrow: What data crosses this boundary? But does Nigeria require all data to remain in Nigeria? This is an area where technology discussions can easily become misleading. The safer answer is: do not reduce Nigerian data law to “everything must be hosted locally.” The NDP Act provides mechanisms for legitimate cross-border personal-data transfers. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s evolving sovereign-cloud programme creates stronger residency and sovereignty requirements for particular government and public-sector workloads. NITDA’s National Cloud Policy 2025 introduced a Cloud First strategy, a national data-classification approach and stronger data-residency requirements. Its accompanying technical guidance is principally targeted at Federal Public Institutions and the cloud providers and integrators serving those environments. ( NITDA ) This distinction matters. A Nigerian fintech deploying an ordinary commercial workload should not blindly copy the architecture of a Federal Government agency handling classified information. Equally, an architect designing a government system should not assume that a standard global SaaS deployment automatically satisfies Nigerian sovereignty requirements. Classification should determine architecture. Design classification into the schema At minimum, an organisation should be able to distinguish: Non-personal Personal Sensitive personal Confidential corporate Public Government-sensitive Restricted/classified The exact taxonomy will depend on the organisation, sector and applicable regulation. This classification can then drive: Encryption Masking RBAC/ABAC Tokenisation Data residency Backup location Logging Retention DLP policies AI access Export restrictions A particularly useful pattern is to move classification into metadata rather than scattering it throughout application code. For example: DataClassification ------------------ ClassificationId Name EncryptionRequired MaskingRequired ExternalAIAllowed CrossBorderAllowed ApprovalRequired MinimumRetention MaximumRetention LoggingLevel Now the security rule follows the classification , rather than requiring every development team to remember every regulation. AI makes this much more urgent Generative AI has dramatically increased the importance of good data modelling. Consider a conventional RAG architecture: Documents ↓ Ingestion ↓ Chunking ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Database ↓ Retrieval ↓ LLM From a data-engineering perspective, it looks reasonable. From a privacy perspective, important information may have disappeared during ingestion. The vector database may know the text of a chunk but not: who the information belongs to why the organisation holds it whether it is sensitive whether it may be used for AI where the original record came from which country the document can be processed in when the source should be deleted who is permitted to retrieve it That creates what I would call compliance-blind RAG . The better model preserves policy metadata throughout ingestion: Chunk ----- ChunkId DocumentId SubjectIds Classification PurposeId AccessPolicyId RetentionPolicyId SourceSystem CountryRestrictions SensitiveDataFlags EmbeddingModel CreatedAt DeleteAfter Retrieval should then be: Query ↓ User/Agent identity ↓ Purpose ↓ Policy filter ↓ Authorised corpus ↓ Hybrid retrieval ↓ LLM rather than: Query ↓ Vector search everything ↓ Hope the LLM behaves GAID explicitly addresses emerging technologies and privacy by design, and the NDPC has repeatedly encouraged developers to embed privacy-preserving technologies and privacy-by-design principles into AI and digital platforms. ( National Drug Policy Committee ) DPIA should be part of architecture governance Under GAID, a Data Privacy Impact Assessment is required where processing is likely to present high risk to people’s rights and freedoms because of its nature, scope, context or purpose. The Directive specifically pays attention to new technologies and high-risk processing. For architects, this means DPIA should happen around the same time as: Architecture Review Security Review Threat Modelling Cloud Review Cost Review — not a week before production release. An architecture decision record could therefore include: ADR-042 ------- Decision: Deploy AI document intelligence service. Personal Data: Yes Sensitive Data: Possible Cross-Border Processing: Yes DPIA Required: Yes Data Residency Review: Required Retention Model: Document policy RP-07 Human Review: Required for high-impact decisions Privacy becomes part of the engineering lifecycle. Breach response also starts with the data model GAID states that where a breach is likely to result in risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms, the controller must notify the Commission within 72 hours of becoming aware of it . Imagine discovering an exposed database and being unable to answer: How many people are affected? What categories of information were exposed? Was sensitive information involved? Which applications accessed the database? Which countries are affected? Which processor was responsible? Those become very difficult questions when data classification and lineage were never modelled. A well-governed catalogue allows incident teams to answer them quickly. GAID additionally expects monitoring, evaluation and maintenance of data-security systems, including activities such as database vulnerability testing, authentication checks, encryption review and software updates. Security controls therefore need to surround the schema — but the schema must also tell security teams what matters most . A practical Nigerian privacy-aware data architecture A modern Nigerian enterprise platform should increasingly be able to connect: DATA SUBJECT │ ▼ Identity Layer │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ ▼                       ▼ Business Records        Consent / Rights │                       │ └───────────┬───────────┘ ▼ Processing Purpose │ ▼ Lawful Basis │ ▼ Classification │ ┌───────────┼────────────┐ ▼           ▼            ▼ Retention     Access       Residency │           │            │ └───────────┼────────────┘ ▼ Data Platform SQL / Lake / SaaS / AI │ ▼ ROPA + Audit Trail Notice what has happened. Compliance has stopped being a document sitting beside the system. It has become part of the system. What I would require in a new Nigerian enterprise data platform For a greenfield platform, my minimum architecture checklist would be: Every personal-data element has a documented purpose and owner; unnecessary fields do not enter the production schema. A data-classification catalogue identifies personal, sensitive and restricted information. Processing purposes are mapped to lawful bases rather than assuming consent covers everything. Consent, where applicable, is versioned and auditable. Subject identifiers allow records to be located across operational databases, data lakes, SaaS platforms and AI stores. Retention policies are machine-readable and capable of driving archival, anonymisation or deletion jobs. Data residency and cross-border transfers are recorded as metadata. Access is both role-aware and purpose-aware. AI/RAG ingestion retains classification and access metadata instead of stripping it away. High-risk processing triggers a DPIA before production. ROPA and compliance reporting should be generated as far as possible from actual platform metadata rather than manually reconstructed. That is a much stronger foundation than beginning with a privacy policy and hoping every system conforms to it. The larger lesson Nigeria’s data-protection framework should not be seen merely as another compliance burden for CIOs. It can force better architecture. Data minimisation reduces storage and breach exposure. Purpose limitation reduces uncontrolled data reuse. Retention policies reduce obsolete data. Classification improves security. Lineage improves analytics and incident response. Structured consent improves customer experience. Cross-border metadata improves cloud governance. Subject identity mapping improves master-data management. Privacy-aware RAG improves enterprise AI. In other words, many of the things regulators want are also things good data architects should already want . The next generation of Nigerian systems should therefore not ask: “How do we make this database NDPA compliant?” The better question is: “How do we design a data platform where compliant behaviour is the default behaviour?” That is the difference between data protection as paperwork and data protection as architecture . And as Nigeria’s enterprises embrace cloud, AI, lakehouses, digital identity and agentic systems, that difference is going to matter enormously. Sources and further reading The primary legal foundation is the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 , administered by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. NDPC — Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 The operational companion is the Nigeria Data Protection Act — General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (GAID) , including guidance covering data-protection principles, DPIAs, security, data-subject rights and cross-border transfers. NDPC — NDP Act GAID 2025 For Nigeria’s broader technology and cloud policy landscape, NITDA maintains its current regulations, standards and cloud-governance instruments. NITDA Regulations and Guidelines This article discusses technology architecture and data-governance practices and should not be treated as legal advice. Sector-specific organisations such as banks, telecoms, healthcare providers and public institutions may have additional regulatory requirements.
